dataset.name: CO2 and CH4 leaf-level fluxes and soil porewater concentrations from common vegetation patches in Louisiana’s coastal wetlands
description: This dataset contains leaf-level flux and soil porewater concentration measurements of carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4 ) in plots in the footprint of Ameriflux sites US-LA2 and US-LA3. Leaf fluxes in US-LA2 were measured on patches dominated by Sagittaria lancifolia and co-dominated by Sagittaria lancifolia and Typha latifolia. In US-LA3, fluxes were measured from distinct Juncus roemerianus and Spartina alterniflora patches. The porewater concentrations were collected across a vertical profile (~50 cm depth) at centric locations within 25 m2 plots where we measured the leaf fluxes. US-LA3 included an additional set of measurements in open water spots. We aimed to evaluate differences in leaf fluxes and porewater pools of CO2 and CH4 of representative ecohydrological patches across a salinity gradient. We also used this dataset to help develop ELM-Wet, a more realistic representation of wetland carbon biogeochemical processes within the U.S. Department of Energy’s Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM) Land Model version 1 (ELM v.1). The files can be opened with regular text editors or spreadsheet programs. Version 2.0 (8/26/2025): This is the latest version of this dataset. The update includes additional samples of soil porewater CH4/CO2 concentrations from June-2021 to November-2022, as well as minor adjustments made to V1 samples via changing Henry's solubility to account for porewater salinity. Additionally leaf-level measurments of spectral indices, PSRI, NDVI, and PRI have been added to complement Leaf-level flux measurements. All V1 data sets have been integrated into V2 sheets, ensuring data from the previous version is contained with the additional samples and consistent with V2 metadata.

spatialCoverage.description: US-LA2: Located off of Lake Salvador WMA, LA, this site is a freshwater flotant marsh (i.e., standing substrate is not attached). The site is primarily dominated by distinct patches of Sagittaria lancifolia and Typha latifolia, with some areas where the two species create a co-dominated patch. For reference, salinity at this site during 2021 averaged 0.16 ppt. More environmental data for the site can be retrieved from: https://cims.coastal.louisiana.gov/Default.aspx; station: CRMS 0224.

US-LA3: This site is located near Lake Hermitage, LA. The site is a mesohaline marsh primarily dominated by Spartina alterniflora and Juncus roemerianus. Salinity during the year 2021 averaged 7.1 ppt. More environmental data for the site can be retrieved from: https://cims.coastal.louisiana.gov/Default.aspx; station: CRMS 3166.

measurementTechnique:
CO2 and CH4 flux measurements at the leaf level were conducted with a portable greenhouse gas analyzer (Picarro G4301) coupled to a custom-made transparent chamber (1654 mL) that was clasped over a leaf or leaf cluster during a 2-minute sampling period. The chambers were fitted with an internal temperature logger (Hobo Pendant Temp Logger), while atmospheric pressure was recorded outside with a portable pressure logger (Hobo U20L Water Level Logger). We sampled four ecohydrological patches, designated according to the dominating species: Sagittaria lancifolia and Sagittaria lancifolia/Typha latifolia at US-LA2, and Juncus roemerianus and Spatina alterniflora at US-LA3. The sampling design consisted of three 25m^2 plots at each patch.
The flux measurements were conducted in different field campaigns between June 2021 and November 2022. Most measurements were conducted between 9:30 a.m. and 3:00 p.m., aiming to capture the part of the day with the highest plant activity.

For each chamber run, we fitted the 2-minute time series of CO2 or CH4 concentrations, C_HM (µmol mol -1), to the non-linear Hutchinson and Moiser one-dimension diffusion model (Hutchinson and Mosier, 1981; Villa et al. 2020a):
C_HM = C_(s ) + (C_0- C_(s) ) e^(-kt) (1)
Where C0 is the initial concentration of CO2 or CH4 in air (µmol mol^-1), Cs is the constant source or sink concentration (µmol mol-1), and k is a curve shape parameter (s-1). C0, Cs, and k were determined by fitting the observed gas concentrations in the chamber over time, t (s), to eq. 1. Flux of CO2 (FCO2) and CH4 (FCH4) at the leaf surface (µmol m_leaf^-2 s^-1) was calculated as:
F=k (C_0- C_(s ) ) (p V)/(R Tch A) (2)
Where p (Pa) is the average atmospheric pressure during each chamber deployment; V is the volume of the chamber (m^3), R is the universal gas constant (8.314 m^3 Pa mol^-1 K^-1), Tch is the average temperature inside the chamber during deployment (K), and A is the on-sided area of leaf enclosed in the chamber (m^2).

Porewater samples for determining CO2 and CH4 concentrations were collected using dialysis samplers, also known as peepers (MacDonald et al., 2013). The peepers consist of 20 cells (61.4 ml) arranged at a 2.8 cm vertical resolution. Each cell has a 22.5 cm2 window screened with a 0.22 µm PES membrane. At least three weeks before the sample, the cells were filled with distilled water to allow equilibration of dissolved gases between concentrations in the porewater. The cells are fitted with two sampling ports with plastic tubing that allow water extraction and refill. We followed the procedure described in Villa et al. (2020a) and Villa et al. (2020b) for sampling every other window. Briefly, a 10 ml water sample was extracted from each cell through the extraction and refill tubing while the other tubing remained connected to a container with N2 to avoid oxygen intrusion. After the sample extraction, the cell was refilled through the same line with deionized water degassed with N2. Samples were placed in 10 ml containers pre-acidified with 0.2 ml HCl 2M, refrigerated, and transported to the laboratory for further processing.

In the laboratory, dissolved CO2 and CH4 concentrations in porewater were measured using the headspace equilibration technique described by Kampbell et al. (1989). We equilibrated 5 ml of sampled water with a 15 ml N2 headspace. Then, we measured concentrations (ppm) in the headspace using an optical spectroscopy analyzer by injecting 2 ml subsamples in a 480 ml injection chamber connected on a close loop with the analyzer.
For each subsample, we calculated the concentration of methane or CO2 in the headspace (Chs - µmol mol^-1) with the following equation:
Chs = (Cai × Vai – Cbi × Vbi) / Vhs (3)
Where Vhs is the volume of the headspace subsample. Cbi and Cai (µmol mol^-1) are the concentrations before and after the injection and after (C_ai – µmol mol^-1) the injections, which were calculated as the mean of 15 measurements before the injection and 15 after the stabilization of the signal, respectively. The volumes before (Vbi) and after (Vai) injections were calculated as follows:
Vbi = Vj + Vi (4)
Vai = Vbi + Vhs (5)
Where Vj (ml) is the volume of the jar (ml), and Vi (ml) is the accumulated volume of injected subsamples (ml).
Lastly, we determined the CO2 and CH4 molar concentrations (mC) in the liquid phase (i.e., porewater) from the measured gas concentrations in the headspace as:
mC =(p_i/RT*Vh+p_i/H_i *Vl)/Vl (6)
Where p_i is the partial pressure of CO2 and CH4, R is the universal gas constant (0.008314 (L MPa K^-1 mol^-1), T is the room temperature (K), Vh is the volume of the headspace (ml), H_i is Henry’s volatility constant for each gas (2.96 and 67.13 L Mpa mol^-1, for CO2 and CH4 respectively), and Vl the volume of the liquid subsample used to create the headspace (i.e., 5 ml).

V2 Update (8/26/2025): Measurements of spectral reflectance were conducted on leaf-chamber subjects after each individual leaf-flux measurement. Spectral sampling was conducted via the use of a portable RGB-NIR leaf spectrometer (CI-710s). Operating as a leaf clip, the segment of plant leaves from within the leaf chamber were sampled for 2s to provide that segment's spectral reflectance. Each leaf sample was measured a minimum of 9 times in different locations on the leaf surface, which were averaged to provide a robust measurement of overall spectral reflectance for the associated sample. Reflectance curves were then used to produce vegetative indices PRI, PSRI, and NDVI. Porewater values in v2 file were adjusted for the solubility of methane and carbon dioxide in salt water, via salinity-dependent Sechenov corrections to Henry’s constant for both gases (Weiss, 1974; Wiesenburg & Guinasso, 1979). Corrections resulted in minimal change (~6% CH4, ~4%CO2), but are an appropriate adjustment in terms of improving overall methods.
